item.title: The Shadow Door: Awkward, abrupt changes
item.content:encoded: The transitions between "base reality" and "storybook reality" are too sudden and awkwardly placed. How does this boy survive being eaten by his bed-turned-monster mouth? How ans why does the father disappear after his son esscapes? And how can s favorite adventuew tale that's existed for decades suddenly act anomolous, without developing s reputation as "the book you'd better not read to kids…especially not by reassuring the kids that it's only fiction"? (Shades of SCP-1241 here…)

item.title: SCP-5000: Why destroy SCP-2000?
item.content:encoded:
This is something i just dont get; i understand why the foundation wants to kill everyone (because of IT, AKA strechy boi), but why destroy SCP-2000? it makes no sense. In order to explain it, i want you to imagine this: Pietro Wilson fails to deliver 055 to 579, the foundation manages to kill everone in the planet thus successfully killing strechy boi and "saving" humanity, but what's next for the foundation? Oh! lets repopulate earth with SCP-2000- oh right… we destroyed it by triggering the yellowstone eruption, not to mention that said eruption might cause a chain reaction that would trigger the rest of the supervolcanoes worldwide… oops.

Also where is the chaos insurgency?

Don't get me wrong, this SCP is great but… Destroying SCP-2000 is confusing… At least for me.

item.title: SCP-5070:
item.content:encoded: It made me laugh a bit and was an enjoyable read, but I happened to find this while researching Site-15, which is the only way I noticed this potential mistake. From the page about foundation sites, Site-15 "specializes in the containment and study of electric, electronic, and computer-based anomalies." because of this, I think it's unlikely that a living stapler would be contained at Site-15. If I were to choose the most suitable containment site for SCP-5070, I would choose Site-76, which is used for containing objects that are presumed to be man-made. If objects confirmed to be man made are not contained in Site-76 then there are other miscellaneous sites with no criteria that i could find. but despite this minor mistake I loved it, especially that interview, it was surprisingly engaging.

item.title: SCP-252-ARC:
item.content:encoded:
-1 from me.

This comes off with the same tone as the gay jokes people threw around in middle school, jokes that I have seen the effects of on my classmates, and it isn't good. What if an LGBT+ kid finds this article and it kills their love of SCP, or it just becomes another dig at their insecurities? Not funny or interesting, comes off as derogatory.

item.title: SCP-2996:
item.content:encoded:
I generally like format screws, but am I really supposed to dig through the edit history here? That's just a bit too much effort for me to bother with when most other format screws on the site require, at most, viewing the page source.

Besides that, since happy endings are relatively rare on this site, I think the ghost girl actually recovering would have been more unexpected than "but it was fake because the Foundation is corrupt and nothing good ever happens there!", which is how the ending came off to me.

item.title: SCP-1179:
item.content:encoded: I don’t think it’s a balrog. If I were down in a burning coal mine fleeing for my life from a giant horned fire monster I wouldn’t stick around long enough to get a good look at it, especially since most of its body is probably obscured by smoke anyway. It’d be easy to confused among all the smoke and fire given off by the creature itself and the burning coal around it, so it’s no surprise that reports vary as to its appearance. A LotR fan is already going to expect a balrog when encountering a fire demon in an abandoned mine, so they’ll be more likely to mistake random shapes in the fire and smoke for wings and the iconic weapons. It’s just human pattern recognition at work.
